candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk IX.1 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

'Let not your heart be troubled (mē tarassesthō): ye believe in God, believe also in me' Cyril notes the deliberate parallel of objects of faith: 'believe in God' and 'believe in me' (pisteuete eis ton Theon, kai eis eme pisteuete). The grammatical symmetry is Christological: faith in God and faith in Christ are not two different acts but one act with one object — the Triune God, in whose self-disclosure the Son is fully God. Against Arian readings that would distinguish 'belief in God' (proper) from 'belief in Christ' (subordinate), Cyril insists the parallel construction excludes any qualitative difference. The verse becomes a creedal pin for Tewahedo Trinitarian dogmatics.

'In my Father's house are many mansions (monai pollai)' Cyril reads with characteristic eschatological precision. The 'many' (pollai) Cyril takes as denying any uniform single eschatological reward: there are differentiated places-of-abiding corresponding to differentiated degrees of holiness attained. Yet he is careful against any Origenist universalism (which would make the differentiation purely educational on a unified upward path): the differentiation is permanent in the eschaton, not transitional. 'Father's house' Cyril reads as the totality of the kingdom, with the 'mansions' (literally 'abiding-places' — monai from menein, to remain) as the differentiated participation each saint has in the one beatific vision. This grounds the Tewahedo doctrine of the differentiated heavenly hierarchy of saints.

Against any reading that would permit alternative access (whether through other religions, through philosophical contemplation, or through natural ethics), Cyril insists on Johannine exclusivity. This verse anchors Tewahedo missiology.

'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' Cyril carefully unpacks against both Sabellian and Arian misreadings. Against Sabellians who would collapse the Persons: the verse does NOT identify the Son AS the Father (Cyril notes the immediate sequel: 'I am in the Father, and the Father in me' preserves the Personal distinction). Against Arians who would subordinate the Son: the verse asserts the Son's perfect representational adequacy — to see Him IS to see the Father, not partially or by analogy but fully and by nature. Cyril notes that the seeing in question is theological perception ('he that hath seen' = he that has truly recognized in faith), not merely physical optics. The verse grounds the Tewahedo iconographic tradition's confidence that depicting Christ's face is legitimate.

'I am in the Father, and the Father in me' (egō en tō Patri, kai ho Patēr en emoi) is for Cyril the foundational Johannine text for what later Greek theology would call perichoresis: the mutual indwelling of the Persons of the Trinity. The reciprocal 'in' (en) preserves the Personal distinction (the Son is not the Father, the Father is not the Son) while affirming the consubstantial unity (each is fully in the other by virtue of the one shared divine essence). 'The words that I speak unto you, I speak not of myself' (continuing the verse) Cyril reads not as denial of personal agency but as expressing the unbroken Trinitarian operation: the Father's words come through the Son in the Spirit. This verse is the textual foundation of Cyril's Trinitarian theology.

'My Father is greater than I' (ho Patēr meizōn mou estin) is THE most contested verse in Cyril's John commentary — the Arian polemical favorite throughout the 4th century, requiring careful orthodox exposition. Cyril resolves through the standard distinction: the verse predicates 'greater' of the Father with respect to the assumed humanity of the incarnate Son, NOT with respect to the eternal divine nature. Insofar as the Son is incarnate (took on human nature), the unincarnate Father is 'greater' in mode-of-existence; insofar as the Son is eternal Word, He is consubstantial-equal with the Father. The verse therefore confirms rather than denies the incarnation, and presupposes rather than undermines the consubstantiality. This careful exposition is one of Cyril's most-cited Johannine passages in later Greek theological tradition.
